newsitem.title: BELGIUM: A guide to the EU's Social Chapter.
newsitem.headline: A guide to the EU's Social Chapter.

text.p: Following are details of the European Union's Social Chapter, which Britain's new Labour government has promised to take on board.
THE SOCIAL CHAPTER: WHAT IS IT?

The official name of the text is the Social Protocol, an annex to the Maastricht Treaty signed by EU countries in 1992. The protocol, which was not signed by London, allows EU countries to bypass Britain and adopt labour laws in areas ranging from worker consultation to social security.
The text also introduced new procedures for adopting workplace rules that allow European labour and management groups to negotiate texts that can then be turned into EU law.
WHAT LAWS HAVE BEEN ADOPTED UNDER THE SOCIAL CHAPTER?

-- The "works council" directive requiring multinational companies with at least 1,000 EU employees, including at least 150 in each of two or more EU countries, to set up procedures for informing and consulting their workers. It took effect in September 1996. Despite London's "opt out", many British multinationals have voluntarily set up a system for consulting their British workers.

-- The "parental leave" directive guaranteeing both men and women three months of unpaid leave at the birth or adoption of a child, along with time off from work for family emergencies. EU countries have until June 3, 1998 to implement it. This was the first EU law to be negotiated by labour and management groups.
WHAT OTHER LAWS ARE ENVISAGED UNDER THE SOCIAL CHAPTER?

-- A directive requiring employers to share the burden of proof with plaintiffs in sex discrimination suits. EU ministers are now debating a text which they are expected to adopt in the second half of the year.

-- Rules to protect part-time workers that are now being negotiated by the Union of Industrial and Employers' Confederations (UNICE), the European Centre of Enterprises with Public Participation (CEEP) and the European Trade Union Confederation.

-- An initiative to fight sexual harassment in the workplace. The Commission has asked labour and management groups to draw up a comprehensive EU policy, but said it might propose legislation if it was not satisfied.
-- Legislation to require national companies to inform and consult their workers. The Commission has promised an initiative but has not yet made a formal proposal.
HAS BRITAIN'S OPT-OUT EXCLUDED IT FROM ALL EU LABOUR LAWS?
No, some EU workplace rules are adopted under provisions of the EU treaty that apply to Britain, for example the controversial "working time" directive setting a 48-hour average maximum work week.
